title: Mamprugu: The Elder Brother of the North

pages.text: Drive north from Tamale and, after Walewale, the flat land ends at a long wall of rock. This is the Gambaga escarpment, a line of cliffs that runs for many kilometres across the north-east of Ghana. On top of it, the air is a little cooler, and the view stretches south across the plains. Two old towns stand close together up here: Gambaga and Nalerigu. In Nalerigu is a palace where chiefs from far away come to be given their authority. The king who sits there is the Nayiri, the ruler of Mamprugu, the kingdom that others call their elder brother.

pages.alt: A long line of rocky cliffs rising above a wide plain of grass and scattered trees.

pages.text: Mamprugu shares its beginning with Dagbon and Nanung. Tradition says that the great chief Naa Gbewaa ruled at Pusiga, near Bawku. When he died, his children quarrelled over who should follow him, and they separated. An elder son, Tohagu, travelled south-west and founded Mamprugu. A younger son, Sitobu, founded Dagbon, and another founded Nanung around Bimbilla. A daughter of the family is remembered in Burkina Faso as the mother of the Mossi kings. Because Tohagu was the senior, his kingdom is honoured as the eldest of the family to this day.

pages.text: For many years the kings of Mamprugu lived at Gambaga. Around 1700, a king named Naa Atabia moved the royal court a few kilometres east to Nalerigu, and there it has stayed. Gambaga remained a busy town of traders and Muslim teachers, on the road that carried kola nuts north and salt and cloth south. Near Nalerigu you can still see the remains of a great wall of mud and stone, said to have been built by an early king to protect people and travellers from raiders. Only a part of it stands today.

pages.text: The word Nayiri means the house of the king, and the title is used for the king himself. A new Nayiri is not simply the son of the last one. He is chosen from among the royal families by a group of elders called kingmakers, who are not princes and cannot become king. As in Dagbon, a chief here sits on skins, and so he is said to be enskinned. Under the Nayiri are chiefs of towns and villages. He also has the right to enskin the chiefs of some neighbouring peoples, a sign of Mamprugu’s long standing in the north-east.

pages.text: Mamprugu was never the largest or richest kingdom of the north. Its strength was respect. When the related kingdoms quarrelled, the Nayiri could be asked to give advice, as an elder brother would. During the colonial period, the British made Gambaga their first headquarters for the north, before they moved to Tamale in 1907. The people lived mainly by farming millet, guinea corn, and yams, by keeping cattle, and by trade. Life followed the rains. Like their neighbours, they celebrate the Damba festival with drumming, dancing, and riders on decorated horses.

pages.text: In 2019, the North East Region was created, and Nalerigu became a regional capital. The old royal town now has a new task. What can Mamprugu teach? In many Ghanaian families, the eldest child is given respect but is also expected to keep the peace, to share, and to speak last and calmly. Being senior is a duty as well as an honour. A kingdom, a class prefect, and an elder sister all face the same test: people keep respecting you only for as long as you use your position to bring others together.

activities.question: Why is Mamprugu called the elder brother among the kingdoms of the north?
options: Tradition says it was founded by the senior son of Naa Gbewaa
It is nearest to the sea

activities.question: What did Naa Atabia do around 1700?
options: He moved the royal court to Nalerigu
He built the port of Tema

activities.question: Who chooses a new Nayiri?
options: Elders called kingmakers, who cannot become king themselves

activities.question: Apply it: Two younger pupils are quarrelling, and a senior pupil is asked to help. Following the lesson of Mamprugu, what should the senior do?
options: Listen to both, stay calm, and help them reach peace

activities.prompt: Put these events in order, from earliest to latest.
items: Naa Atabia moves the court to Nalerigu
The British move their northern headquarters from Gambaga to Tamale
Nalerigu becomes the capital of the North East Region
